Vignette: Fatima, Age 69

Fatima came to this country from Lebanon more than thirty years ago, building a quiet life with her husband in a mid-sized American city. She raised her children, learned English through persistence and necessity, and when her youngest left home, she took a part-time job at a fast food restaurant near her neighborhood - not because she needed the income badly, but because she needed the movement, the routine, the small dignities of being useful. She has worked the morning shift there for eleven years. Her coworkers are decades younger than she is, and she has always liked that. It kept her feeling present in the world.

Three years ago, a man began coming into the restaurant every morning and sitting in the same corner booth. At first Fatima thought nothing of it. Regulars were common. But he began timing his visits to her shifts specifically, and she noticed. He would watch her. When she moved to wipe tables, he moved his eyes. When she spoke to other customers, his jaw tightened. He began leaving her notes folded beneath his coffee cup - first compliments, then declarations, then something that felt like ownership. When she stopped acknowledging him, the notes became threatening. He began appearing outside her bus stop. Once, he followed her two blocks toward her home before she ducked into a pharmacy, hands shaking, and called her husband.

The police were involved. The man was warned, eventually charged. He moved away, or at least disappeared from her immediate life. Legally, the situation resolved. Inside Fatima, nothing resolved at all.

She still works the morning shift, though her husband now drives her and waits in the parking lot until she is inside. She will not take the bus anymore. The corner booth where the man used to sit remains empty most mornings, and Fatima cannot look at it directly. She routes her cleaning path around it. When a male customer lingers too long over his coffee, her chest tightens and her hands go cold and she finds reasons to stay behind the counter. She has never told her manager why she sometimes needs a moment in the back room, standing with her palms pressed flat against the stainless steel counter, steadying herself.

At home, she sleeps poorly. She wakes between two and four in the morning and lies still, listening to sounds in the hallway, certain for a few disorienting seconds that someone is in the house. Her husband has learned not to reach for her suddenly in the dark. Once, he touched her shoulder to wake her and she screamed - a sound she says she did not recognize as her own. She has not told her adult children the full extent of what happened. In her understanding of herself, in the culture she carries inside her, a woman her age is supposed to have moved past vulnerability. She feels a deep shame about this that she has difficulty naming.

She describes herself as someone who used to enjoy people. She was the woman who remembered customers' names, who asked after their children. Now she finds herself scanning faces for threat before she sees them as human. She has stopped attending her mosque's women's group, which she loved for years, because the walk there requires passing an alley that reminds her of the pharmacy doorway where she hid. The memory lives in her body as much as in her mind - a particular quality of cold in her fingers, a narrowing behind her sternum.

What she says she wants most is to stop feeling like she is still waiting for him to come back. She knows, intellectually, that he is gone. But some part of her - the part that wakes at three in the morning and listens - does not believe it yet. She is sixty-nine years old, she says, and she did not expect to spend these years being afraid.
